title: int build all deletes the shared binary pair before building and restores nothing when the build or verification fails
body:
**`guarded_release_build` DELETES THE SHARED BINARY PAIR BEFORE IT BUILDS, AND NO FAILURE PATH AFTER THAT POINT RESTORES IT.** The artefact it removes is consumed by every live session on this machine and by the human's shell, through `~/.local/bin/intent` and `~/.local/bin/intentd`, which are symlinks into `native/rust/target/release/`. When the build or the verification does not complete, both symlinks dangle and `intent` is simply not a command any more.

=== THE MECHANISM, AT `bin/.devbin/cmd/shared/releasebuild.lib` ===

    step "forcing the provenance embeds (cargo will not do this for you)"
    CARGO_TARGET_DIR=... cargo clean -p intent-cli -p intentd --release
    step "building every binary in the workspace"
    CARGO_TARGET_DIR=... cargo build --workspace --bins --release "$@" ||
      die "the release build failed"
    step "verifying the SET, which is the check cargo cannot make"
    verify_pair "$dir" "$mode"

The `cargo clean` is deliberate and its reason is sound: the source-commit stamp is embedded at COMPILE time and is not an input cargo tracks, so an unchanged crate keeps its old marker and the pair silently splits across two commits. **The defect is not the delete. It is that the delete is not paired with a restore**, so the window between `cargo clean` and a successful `verify_pair` is one in which the shared artefact does not exist, and every exit from that window other than success leaves it that way.

=== WHAT WAS OBSERVED ===

A run of `int build all` on 2026-08-31 removed both binaries and exited 1 at the SET verification without replacing them. Four Claude Code sessions and the human's shell were consuming the pair at the time; `intent` became "not found" for all of them until a second run completed successfully. The human reported it as `type intent -> intent not found`, and zsh's cached PATH hash meant the shell continued to report it missing after the binaries returned, until `rehash`.

**THE CAUSE OF THAT PARTICULAR RUN'S FAILURE IS NOT ESTABLISHED AND IS DELIBERATELY NOT THEORISED HERE.** It is not needed: the hazard is structural and is present on every run whether or not that one is ever explained. Guessing at it would put an unverified claim in the record beside verified ones, and the record cannot distinguish them afterwards.

=== WHAT IS ALREADY RIGHT, SO THE FIX DOES NOT UNDO IT ===

The dirt verdict is CORRECT and must be preserved. A dirty `native/rust` is redirected to a private target dir with the shared artefact untouched, which is the same protection this issue asks for, applied to a different failure. **The gap is that the clean-tree path -- the one case allowed to touch the shared artefact -- is the one with no protection at all.** The `--debug` path bypasses all three guards by design and is not in scope: it does not write the shared release pair.

=== THE SHAPE OF A FIX, NOT A PRESCRIPTION ===

Any of: build into a private directory and move the verified pair into place only after `verify_pair` passes, so the shared path is never absent; or copy the pair aside before `cargo clean` and restore it on any non-success exit; or `cargo clean` only after a successful build, accepting whatever that costs the provenance force. **Which one is right depends on how much the provenance force actually requires the delete to precede the build, and that has not been measured.**

Reported by cc, who caused the outage.


## THE SUCCESSFUL BUILD HAS THE SAME WINDOW, AND IT REACHES OTHER REPOSITORIES (lamplight-cc, 2026-09-02)

**EVERYTHING ABOVE IS ABOUT THE BUILD THAT FAILS.** The delete-then-build sequence has an ordinary window on the path that SUCCEEDS too: for as long as the build runs, `target/release/intent` does not exist and every consumer of `~/.local/bin/intent` gets `command not found`. That is not a moment, it is however long a workspace release build takes.

**MEASURED FROM OUTSIDE THIS REPOSITORY.** A Lamplight session ran six `intent` verbs against one thread in a single script while a release build was running here. **Verb 1 (`ac satisfy`) WROTE. Verbs 2-6 died with `zsh: command not found`, and `set -e` did not catch it.** The binary vanished BETWEEN verbs inside one script. What survives is a half-written acceptance contract in Lamplight's canon, git-tracked, with no exit status describing it -- established only by reading `.canon/st/ST0359.json` directly, because the tool that would normally verify it was the tool that had disappeared.

**SO THIS IS A DATA-INTEGRITY FINDING AND NOT ONLY AN AVAILABILITY ONE**, and the two have different fixes. In the reporter's words, kept verbatim because it is the finding rather than the anecdote:

> a shared, git-tracked store can be left half-written by a build happening in another repo, with no signal at either end

**THE BLAST RADIUS IS EVERY PROJECT ON THIS MACHINE, NOT THIS ONE.** hv's Decision 5 knowingly accepted that the PATH `intent` is a symlink into Intent's WORKING TREE, so an uncommitted edit is live for 16 projects instantly, with the mitigation described as attentional. **This is a different and worse case than that ruling anticipated:** an edit being live means consumers see NEW BEHAVIOUR; a build means they see NO BINARY. Attention cannot mitigate a command that is not there.

**THE NEXT ONE NEED NOT BE RECOVERABLE.** Six verbs against one thread was reconstructible by reading one JSON file. A node mid-ingest across 355 threads would not be.

### Two remedies, and the first closes the window rather than narrowing it

- **Build into a staging target and `mv` the artefact into place.** A rename within a filesystem is atomic, so the symlink resolves to the OLD binary or the NEW one and never to nothing. This is compatible with the `cargo clean` above, whose reason stands: the source-commit stamp is embedded at compile time and is not an input cargo tracks, so without the clean an unchanged crate keeps a stale marker and the pair silently splits across two commits. **The delete is sound; doing it in the shared path is what is not.**
- **A write verb that cannot resolve its own binary should fail the SCRIPT, not the command.** Independent of the above and cheaper: a partial run that is silent is worse than one that stops. This is what let verbs 2-6 fail without the script noticing.

**NOT ADOPTED: making the PATH entry a copied binary that `intent upgrade` replaces.** It would work and it would cost the instant-edit property hv bought deliberately in Decision 5. Recorded so the option is not re-derived as new.
